title: When should Revenue Multiple be used?
subtitle: The last resort when a company has no profit yet to value it by
openingQuestion: A tech startup is growing revenue 100%/year but is still losing money (no positive EBITDA or profit). Which valuation metric can still be applied?
openingOptions: P/E, because it always applies to every company
No metric at all can be applied to a loss-making company
EV/Revenue (Revenue Multiple) - because revenue is always positive even when the company has no profit yet, allowing a rough comparison, though less accurate than profit-based metrics
P/B is the only viable option
explanation: EV/Revenue (or Price/Sales) = Enterprise Value / Revenue. When a company has no positive profit yet (common at growth-stage tech startups), profit-based metrics (P/E, EV/EBITDA) become meaningless. Revenue Multiple is a usable option because revenue is rarely negative - but it's the least accurate metric of all since it completely ignores profitability and cost.

diagram.label: The company has no profit yet

realWorldExample.description: SaaS (Software-as-a-Service) companies at an early stage are usually valued using EV/Revenue (e.g. 5-10 times annual recurring revenue - ARR) because most have no positive profit yet, despite very fast revenue growth.

quiz.question: Why is Revenue Multiple considered the least reliable valuation metric compared to P/E or EV/EBITDA?
options: Because revenue is harder to forecast than profit so the multiple is less stable
Because revenue is always inflated in published financial statements
Because revenue says nothing about margin or cost efficiency
Revenue Multiple is actually more accurate than other valuation metrics
quiz.explanation: Revenue is just the 'top line', not reflecting cost, margin, or operating efficiency. Two companies with 1,000 billion in revenue, one hugely profitable and one deeply loss-making, would carry the same multiple.

quiz.question: Two SaaS startups both have EV/Revenue = 8x, but startup A has an 80% gross margin while startup B only has 30%. Does this equal multiple correctly reflect the two companies' relative value?
options: Yes, since an equal Revenue multiple means the two companies are equally valuable
B is always better than A because a lower margin shows more competitive pricing
Gross margin has nothing at all to do with reading a Revenue Multiple
No - an equal multiple means A is being relatively undervalued
quiz.explanation: This is exactly the biggest limitation of Revenue Multiple: it completely ignores margin - two companies with the same Revenue multiple but very different margins have very different real economic value.

quiz.question: When are you forced to use EV/Revenue instead of other multiples?
options: When the business has no profit or positive EBITDA yet
When the business carries too much long-term debt
When the business operates in multiple different countries
When the business just completed a large merger
quiz.explanation: A negative denominator makes every profit-based multiple meaningless. Revenue is the only line still positive at an early-stage startup, so it gets used - even though it says nothing about whether the business will ever be profitable.

quiz.question: Why is EV/Revenue the least reliable of the multiples?
options: Because revenue is the figure most easily adjusted by accounting
Because it completely ignores the business's ability to turn a profit
Because it only applies to businesses in the tech industry
Because revenue changes with the season so it can't be compared
quiz.explanation: Two businesses with the same 100 billion in revenue, one with an 80% margin, one with 5%, give the same EV/Revenue but very different real value, differing by dozens of times. This multiple only measures scale, not quality.

quiz.question: Two SaaS startups both have EV/Revenue of 8x, with gross margins of 80% and 40%. Which one is more valuable?
options: The two are equivalent since they share the same revenue multiple
The 40%-margin one, since it still has more room to improve margin
The 80%-margin one, because it keeps more of every dong earned
Can't be determined without knowing the growth rate
quiz.explanation: At the same price relative to revenue, one side turns 80 dong into potential profit, the other only 40. This is exactly the flaw in a revenue-based multiple - it treats the two businesses as identical.

keyTakeaways: EV/Revenue: used when a company has no positive profit yet to apply other metrics
The least accurate metric because it completely ignores profitability
Common in valuing growth-stage tech startups

practicePrompt.question: A tech startup is growing revenue 100%/year but is still losing money (negative EBITDA, negative Net Income) because it's burning cash to expand its market. An analyst can't use P/E or EV/EBITDA to value this company. Which metric should they use instead, and why?
options: EV/Revenue: used when a company has no positive profit yet, because revenue is rarely negative
P/B should be used instead, as it's the only metric applicable to a loss-making company
No metric at all is suitable for valuing a loss-making company, so valuation should be skipped
Wait until the company turns a profit before starting to value it at all - don't value a company still in a loss-making stage
practicePrompt.explanation: EV/Revenue: used when a company has no positive profit yet, to substitute for metrics like P/E or EV/EBITDA. Revenue is rarely negative, so it can still be calculated and compared across industries, even though this metric reflects real profitability far less than EV/EBITDA.

summary.keyIdea: EV/Revenue: used when a company has no positive profit yet, to substitute for other metrics
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: The least accurate metric because it completely ignores profitability

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: The lesson already has a real example comparing revenue-based valuation (startup) against P/E-based valuation (FPT) - see the 'Real example' section above. Now find a tech startup yourself and estimate its revenue multiple.
application.secondary: Remember this is the least accurate metric - use it only when no better option is available.

sections.text: When a company hasn't earned a single dong of profit yet, P/E and EV/EBITDA become meaningless. This is when analysts are forced to reach for the last resort: Revenue Multiple.

EV/Revenue (or Price/Sales) = Enterprise Value / Revenue. When a company has no positive profit yet - common at growth-stage tech startups - profit-based metrics become meaningless or negative. Revenue is rarely negative, so Revenue Multiple becomes the usable option. Early-stage SaaS companies are usually valued this way at 5-10 times annual recurring revenue (ARR).
The price of simplicity: ignoring margin entirely

Revenue is just the 'top line', not reflecting cost, margin, or operating efficiency. Two companies both with 1,000 billion in revenue but one with a 30% gross margin and the other with 80% - if both trade at the same EV/Revenue = 8x, the 80%-margin startup is actually being priced 'cheap' relative to its real profit potential, while the 30%-margin startup may be priced above its true value. This is the biggest limitation of Revenue Multiple: it completely ignores the ability to turn revenue into profit.

items: Only use it when P/E and EV/EBITDA aren't available (a company without profit yet)
Always pair Revenue Multiple with gross margin when comparing companies
The least accurate of the commonly used valuation multiples
Common in valuing tech startups, especially the SaaS model

sections.text: A real example: why a startup without profit yet still gets valued by revenue

items: A growth-stage tech startup is usually losing money or has near-zero profit - P/E can't be used (since E is near zero or negative), so investors turn to Revenue Multiple (company value / revenue) instead
A contrasting example: FPT (an already profitable company) is valued using P/E of about 10.5x rather than a revenue multiple, because FPT's profit is stable and predictable enough
A high or low revenue multiple depends on expected growth rate and future potential margin, not current revenue

sections.label: How to apply this yourself
sections.text: Find recent fundraising news for a Vietnamese startup (which usually discloses a company valuation), and cross-reference it with the publicly disclosed revenue (if available) to calculate the revenue multiple yourself (Revenue Multiple = Valuation / Revenue).

lines: Revenue Multiple is a tool born of insufficient information - use it when you must, but don't forget it leaves out the most important part: profit.
